description: I’m a Computer Science Engineering student passionate about technology, problem-solving, and innovation. My goal is to build an AI-powered solution that addresses a real-world problem. I’m looking for motivated teammates skilled in programming, AI/ML, web development, UI/UX design, or research. Let’s combine our strengths, turn ideas into reality, and create something impactful together!
summary:
What we developed: Earth Jukebox is an interactive web app that turns images of our changing planet into music. Users pick a view of Earth and press play. A playhead reads the image from left to right, and the pixels it passes decide the sound. Height sets pitch, brightness sets which notes play and how loud, and color saturation shapes the tone. A year slider (2000-2025) and a time-lapse mode let users hear how the planet changes over time. Users can also upload their own Earth data frame to hear it.
How it addresses the challenge: Earth data is usually shown only as images and charts. We made it something people can hear as well as see. The sonification rules are simple and consistent, so listeners can learn to recognize patterns in the data.
Why it matters: Sound makes Earth science more accessible, including for visually impaired users, and makes climate change easier to feel and remember. It invites students and the public to explore NASA Earth data with curiosity.
details:
What it does and how it works: Earth Jukebox turns images of our changing planet into music. The user picks a view of Earth and presses play. A playhead reads the image left to right, and the pixels it passes decide the sound. The frame is split into eight latitude bands, and higher bands play higher notes. Only bright, changing regions sound, and brighter pixels play louder. Color saturation opens the sound filter, so vivid color sounds bright and washed-out color sounds muted. The average brightness of the whole frame sets the tempo and a low drone. A year slider (2000-2025) and a time-lapse mode let users hear the planet change over time. The page shows live readouts of tempo, mode, and "planet energy."

Benefits: It makes Earth data accessible to people who learn by listening, including visually impaired users. It turns complex imagery into something simple and memorable, and it lets anyone compare years by ear.

Intended impact: We want to raise public awareness of how our planet is changing, help students and educators explore NASA Earth data in a new way, and show that data can be experienced as well as viewed.

Tools and technologies: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, running entirely in the browser with no installation or special hardware. [Add: HTML Canvas for reading pixels, Web Audio API for sound, if that's what app.js uses.]

Creativity: The image itself is the musical score. Instead of charts, users hear data, and every rule maps a visual property to a musical one in a consistent way. Users can also load their own frame and hear it with the same rules.

Factors we considered: Accessibility, since sound opens the data to more people. Simplicity, since four clear rules mean listeners can learn to "read" the music. Scientific grounding, since the frames are shaped like NASA Earth Information Center datasets and real frames play with the same rules. Our built-in frames are stylized stand-ins, and we were open about that.
